query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Thermal cycling of pre-passivated Q235 steel induces non-uniform expansion and contraction of the passivation film, leading to microcrack formation that locally exposes the substrate, thereby increasing overall corrosion rates under aggressive conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 steel with a homogeneous passivation film created by standard pickling/passivation (per PMC9504384).
generation.intervention: Subject samples to repeated thermal cycles between room temperature and 700 °C (e.g., 10 cycles), simulating thermal stress fluctuations.
generation.conditions: After thermal cycling, expose samples to a corrosive salt environment at elevated temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Microcracks and delamination within the passivation film created by thermal cycling act as channels for electrolyte ingress.
generation.mechanism: Differential thermal expansion between the steel substrate and the passivation film causes mechanical stresses that exceed the adhesion limits of the film, leading to microcracking and spallation, which accelerates corrosion processes.
generation.predicted_outcome: Thermally cycled samples will demonstrate a higher corrosion rate (approximately 25–35% increase in weight loss and more extensive localized attack) compared to non-cycled control samples when subjected to identical corrosive exposures.
generation.baseline: Passivated Q235 steel that is held at a constant temperature (no thermal cycling) before salt exposure.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be pronounced only when the thermal gradients are sufficiently large; minimal cycling or reduced thermal differentials should not produce the effect.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the effect may depend on the cycling rate and the inherent mechanical properties of the native passivation film, which can vary.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of passivated Q235 steel samples; subject one set to 10 complete thermal cycles between room temperature and 700 °C, while the control set is maintained at room temperature. Then, expose both sets to the same high-temperature salt aggressive environment.
measurements: Microscopic analysis (SEM) for microcrack density and morphology
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermal cycled samples do not show a statistically significant increase in microcracking and corrosion rate (relative to controls), the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, the corrosion behavior and mechanism of Q235 in atmospheric environment are studied by designing a cyclic salt spray accelerated corrosion experiment. The specific conclusions are as follows: Q235 low-carbon steel in the atmospheric environment of the accelerated corrosion process can be roughly divided into four stages: (1) passivation film corrosion product generation and local shedding, (2) matrix rust layer generation and covering, (3) rust layer accumulation and stacking onto a flat and dense second protective layer, and (4) matrix rust layer breaking through the protective layer continues to grow thicker until shedding. After pickling passivation treatment of Q235 low-carbon steel in the atmospheric environment of corrosion from passivation film weakness, pitting corrosion gradually develops into comprehensive corrosion with the elongation of time. Rust layer composition gradually transitions from passivation products into iron oxide based on hydroxyl iron oxide. The whole process is “from point to surface” corrosion. In this study, the passivation behavior of Q235 carbon steel at different temperatures of 20 °C, 40 °C, and 60 °C was studied. The specific conclusions are as follows:(1)The passivation process was divided into a rapid passivation phase before 24 h and a stable passivation phase after 24 h. Among them, the early passivation rate was faster at 40 °C and 60 °C, indicating that the increase in temperature accelerated the formation of the passive film.(2)Under different temperature conditions, the passive film products are not the same, and more Fe2O3 is produced with an increase in temperature—which is the main reason for the temperature increases—and the passive film is better and thicker.(3)After passivation, the semiconductor properties of the passive films formed are the same. At a temperature of 20 °C, the capacitance of the passive film after passivation is significantly smaller than that at 40 and 60 °C. As the temperature increases, better passivated films form.

papers.title: Research on the Corrosion Behavior of Q235 Pipeline Steel in an Atmospheric Environment through Experiment.
papers.system: Passivated Q235 low‐carbon (pipeline) steel in atmospheric, cyclic salt spray environment
papers.approach: Cyclic salt spray accelerated corrosion tests with weight loss measurements, macroscopic/microscopic observations and elemental (EDS) analyses
papers.findings: The intact passivation film initially forms a protective barrier; however, after several days the film locally corrodes and detaches, leading to pitting and a transition to a mixed rust layer. Corrosion kinetics follow a four‐stage process with variations in passivation film failure and subsequent substrate corrosion.
papers.mechanism: Degradation is driven by the breakdown of the passivation layer under chloride attack, where film rupture exposes the substrate to corrosive species; additionally, the formation of new rust products and accumulation of a matrix rust layer provides a secondary, though incomplete, protective effect.

papers.title: Effective Corrosion Inhibition of Carbon Steel in Hydrochloric Acid by Dopamine-Produced Carbon Dots.
papers.system: Pre-exposed Q235 carbon steel in 1 M HCl solution
papers.approach: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, potentiodynamic polarization, and weight loss measurements in the presence of nitrogen-doped carbon dots (NCDs) as inhibitors
papers.findings: Increasing NCD concentration, exposure time, and temperature results in higher inhibition efficiencies (up to ~96%), attributed to the formation of an effective, adsorbed protective layer on the steel surface.
papers.mechanism: The protective mechanism is proposed to occur via adsorption of NCDs on the Q235 steel surface following Langmuir isotherm behavior, which effectively blocks active sites and retards corrosive reactions.

papers.title: The Effect of Temperatures on the Passivation Behavior of Q235 Steel in the Simulated Concrete Pore Solution.
papers.system: Q235 steel immersed in simulated concrete pore solution under varying temperatures (20°C, 40°C, 60°C)
papers.approach: Electrochemical measurements (EIS, MS curves) to follow passivation film formation over time under controlled temperature conditions
papers.findings: Passivation occurs in two distinct stages – a rapid initial formation (within 24 h) and a stable phase thereafter. Higher temperatures accelerate the formation and impact the composition (favoring Fe3+ compounds like Fe2O3) and impedance properties of the passive film.
papers.mechanism: Temperature influences the kinetics of passive film growth by promoting the rapid oxidation of iron species; while higher temperatures yield thicker, more stoichiometrically distinct films, they may also alter the protective quality if phase transformations (e.g., from hydroxides to oxides) become detrimental under extreme conditions.

papers.title: High-Temperature Corrosion of Ni-Cr-Mo Cladding Layers with Different Si Contents in NaCl-KCl-Na2SO4-K2SO4
papers.system: Q235 steel substrates modified via laser-cladded Ni-Cr-Mo corrosion-resistant cladding layers (with varied Si contents)
papers.approach: Laser cladding of corrosion-resistant alloys followed by weight loss tests and characterization (XRD, SEM) after exposure in high-temperature molten salt environments at 550°C
papers.findings: Si additions improve the formation of a dense Cr-oxide scale, resulting in significantly reduced corrosion rates (e.g., with 5 wt.% Si, the corrosion rate was only 38.2% of the unmodified layer's rate).
papers.mechanism: Enhanced corrosion protection derives from the rapid formation and retention of a Cr-rich oxide scale that acts as a barrier under high-temperature conditions, limiting oxygen and salt penetration.

papers.title: Effect of Ti Content on the Microstructure and Corrosion Resistance of CoCrFeNiTix High Entropy Alloys Prepared by Laser Cladding.
papers.system: High entropy alloy (HEA) coatings (CoCrFeNiTix) applied via laser cladding on Q235 steel
papers.approach: Preparation of HEA coatings with varied Ti content; evaluation via microstructural analyses, hardness tests, and corrosion tests in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution
papers.findings: Higher Ti content results in a more complex phase composition including FCC and intermetallic phases; these microstructural changes lead to increased hardness and improved resistance to pitting corrosion compared with the base Q235 steel.
papers.mechanism: Protective effects are achieved through the formation of a dendritic structure with segregated phases that promote the development of chemically stable, corrosion-resistant intermetallic compounds on the steel surface.

established: Pre-exposure Q235 steel typically features a passivation film that provides initial protection, but its integrity can be compromised in aggressive environments.
Temperature influences both the kinetics and the composition of passive films on Q235 steel, affecting its overall corrosion resistance.
Inhibitor additives (organic or inorganic) can improve corrosion resistance by forming adsorbed protective layers with well-defined adsorption kinetics (often described by the Langmuir model).

approaches_tried.approach: Salt spray accelerated corrosion on passivated Q235 steel
approaches_tried.outcome: Revealed a four-stage corrosion process with initial protection followed by film rupture and substrate attack

approaches_tried.approach: Application of adsorptive inhibitors (NCDs, CLS) under controlled solution chemistries
approaches_tried.outcome: Significantly increased inhibition efficiencies through formation of protective adsorption films

approaches_tried.approach: Laser cladding of corrosion-resistant HEA coatings or Ni-Cr-Mo layers on Q235 steel
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced high-temperature corrosion resistance by modifying the surface chemistry and structure, particularly through oxide scale formation

approaches_tried.approach: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy at varying temperatures in simulated pore solutions
approaches_tried.outcome: Elucidated the temperature dependence of passive film formation and its electrochemical properties

mechanisms: Integrity and breakdown of the initial passivation film govern the transition from corrosion protection to aggressive degradation.
Adsorption of inhibitor species (e.g., carbon dots, CLS) onto the steel surface blocks active corrosion sites.

High temperature promotes transformation of the passive film composition (e.g., formation of Fe3+ oxides or Cr-rich oxide scales) which can either enhance or compromise protection depending on film integrity.
disagreements: Some studies find that increasing temperature accelerates passivation (improving protection), while others suggest that higher temperatures lead to film rupture and loss of protection.
The relative importance of bulk phase modifications (via alloying or cladding) versus surface film integrity in dictating overall corrosion resistance remains debated.
open_questions: What is the dominant mechanistic factor controlling the transition from passivation-based protection to degradation in Q235 steel across room- and high-temperature regimes?
How do the microstructural initial conditions of the pre-exposure passivation film affect its high-temperature behavior and response to subsequent corrosive salt exposure?
Can annealing or other thermal treatments that simulate high-temperature regimes change the chemical nature of the passivation film in a predictable manner?
opportunities: Conduct a controlled study where pre-exposure Q235 steel (with a characterized passivation film) is subjected to an annealing treatment at high temperatures (e.g., 700–900 °C) in an inert atmosphere to isolate the effects of film transformation, followed by salt spray or molten salt exposure.
Compare samples with and without the pre-existing passivation film to determine if retention of the film correlates with reduced corrosion rates and altered corrosion kinetics.

Utilize in situ electrochemical and surface analytical techniques (e.g., EIS, XPS) to monitor film transformation and correlate phase changes with electrochemical protection; a falsifying observation would be if the pre-exposed passivated steel, after annealing, shows no difference in corrosion behavior relative to an unpassivated control, undermining the film integrity hypothesis.

directions.direction: Thermal transformation of the pre-existing passivation film on Q235 steel.
directions.type: Heat or thermomechanical treatment and microstructure control
directions.assessment: Directly addresses the degradation/retention mechanism by linking film composition/morphology changes upon annealing to subsequent corrosion behavior. The physics of oxide transformations are well supported (PMC9867134, PMC9504384) and the study is experimentally feasible in controlled inert and salt‐spray environments.

directions.direction: Role of chloride adsorption on the native passivation film in triggering localized corrosion mechanisms.
directions.assessment: Targets the adsorption of aggressive species (chloride ions) on the film that may prompt pitting. The mechanism is supported by observations of film rupture and pitting (PMC9504384, PMC7570617) and can be isolated by controlling chloride concentration at ambient and elevated temperatures.

directions.direction: Influence of thermal cycling on film uniformity and microcrack formation in the passivation layer.
directions.type: Processing or synthesis route with controlled thermal cycling combined with microstructural analysis
directions.assessment: Focuses on how repeated thermal stresses cause microcracking and loss of film integrity, thereby reducing corrosion protection. Experimental implementation via cyclic heating (room to high temperature) is achievable with available instrumentation and is supported by evidence on passivation film breakdown (PMC9504384).

directions.direction: Variation in substrate microstructure (grain boundary heterogeneity) affecting passivation film adhesion and subsequent corrosion kinetics.
directions.type: Composition design coupled with microstructure control and characterization
directions.assessment: Explores the role of inherent microstructural variations in Q235 steel on local film formation and its durability under corrosive conditions. While more indirect, it can be probed by correlating grain structure with corrosion damage; literature (PMC9504384, PMC9867134) provides precedent for heterogeneous film behavior although disagreements remain regarding dominant factors.

candidates.hypothesis: Annealing-induced thermal transformation of the native passivation film on Q235 steel converts protective hydroxide phases into less adherent Fe3+ oxides, which under subsequent salt spray exposure at 700–900 °C leads to accelerated corrosion relative to non-annealed samples.
candidates.intervention: Subjecting the pre-passivated steel to an annealing treatment in an inert atmosphere at either 700 °C or 900 °C for a controlled duration (e.g., 1 hour).

candidates.hypothesis: Pre-adsorption of chloride ions on the native passivation film of Q235 steel facilitates localized pitting corrosion at high temperatures by destabilizing the film, whereas samples pre-treated to minimize chloride adsorption retain protection.
candidates.intervention: Expose one set of samples to a low-concentration chloride solution (e.g., dilute NaCl) at room temperature to induce controlled chloride adsorption, while a control set is rinsed thoroughly; then subject both sets to high-temperature salt exposure (700–900 °C).

candidates.hypothesis: Thermal cycling of pre-passivated Q235 steel induces non-uniform expansion and contraction of the passivation film, leading to microcrack formation that locally exposes the substrate, thereby increasing overall corrosion rates under aggressive conditions.
candidates.intervention: Subject samples to repeated thermal cycles between room temperature and 700 °C (e.g., 10 cycles), simulating thermal stress fluctuations.

candidates.hypothesis: Inherent substrate microstructural heterogeneity in Q235 steel leads to spatial variation in passivation film adhesion, such that regions with high grain boundary density form weaker films that preferentially delaminate under high-temperature, corrosive conditions, resulting in localized accelerated corrosion.
candidates.intervention: Apply a mild, controlled annealing treatment aimed at accentuating the differences in grain boundary character without altering the overall passivation process, then form the typical passivation film using standard procedures.

minor_issues: Extrapolates from passivation studies at lower temperatures (up to ~60 °C) to 700–900 °C conditions without direct corroborating data for these higher temperatures.

Claims that Fe3+ oxides formed at high annealing temperatures are less adherent than hydroxides but does not cite specific literature on oxidation/spallation behavior of Q235 steel in the 700–900 °C range.
fixes: Incorporate references or preliminary data specifically addressing oxide scale adhesion and spallation for Q235 in the 700–900 °C regime.
Clarify how the proposed hydroxide-to-oxide phase transformation is confirmed at high temperatures (e.g., by thermogravimetric, XRD, or in situ microscopy methods).
evidence_needs: High-temperature oxidation experiments on Q235 to validate oxide phase evolution and adhesion at 700–900 °C.
In situ or ex situ surface analysis (e.g., XPS, XRD) before and after annealing to confirm transformations in the passivation film and their correlation with corrosion rates.
